opus-5.5.text:
When I first joined, what struck me most was how focused the place felt. Coming from a physics background, I was used to environments where people chase whatever is interesting at the moment. At Anthropic there was a very clear sense of what people thought mattered: building models that are genuinely capable, and taking seriously the question of whether we can make them safe and understandable as they get more powerful.

It also felt smaller and more tightly knit than I expected. People from very different backgrounds, physics, neuroscience, software engineering, policy, were sitting together and arguing about the same problems. There wasn't much hierarchy in the discussions. If you had a good idea or a good piece of evidence, people listened, no matter how long you'd been there.

Another thing that surprised me was how empirical the culture was. There's a lot of talk outside about "AI safety" as something philosophical. But inside, the attitude was: let's measure it, let's run the experiment, let's see what the model actually does. That resonated with me, because it felt like doing science again, except the object of study is something we're building ourselves and it changes every few months.

And honestly, there was a bit of a feeling that things were moving very fast, faster than most people outside realized. You'd see capabilities improve in ways that made you rethink your timelines. That gave the work a sense of urgency, but also a lot of responsibility. So my first impression was a mix of excitement and seriousness, a group of people who believed this technology is going to be very important and wanted to get it right.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, when I first joined, my impression was that Anthropic felt less like a company and more like a research lab that happened to have a very good product attached to it. Coming from the outside, you see the headlines, the models, the safety messaging, and you form a picture that's quite abstract. Once I was inside, what struck me first was how much of the organization was oriented around a small number of very concrete questions: how do you make a model that is genuinely useful as an agent, how do you understand what it's actually doing internally, and how do you do both without losing control of the thing you're building.

The second impression was the density of people who had thought seriously about agents before "agents" became the word everyone used. For me that mattered a lot, because my own work on ReAct and on language agents was always about this loop between reasoning and acting, and I'd spent years feeling like I was explaining why that loop was the right unit of analysis. At Anthropic I didn't have to explain it. People were already arguing about the next layer of the problem, like how you evaluate long-horizon behavior, or how you keep a model honest when it's operating with tools over many steps.

The third thing, which I think people underestimate from outside, is how much the safety culture is a technical culture rather than a compliance culture. I expected something closer to a review board. Instead, it was more like a shared research taste. The question "what could go wrong here" came up in the same breath as "how do we make this stronger," and the same people were asking both. That shaped how I thought about my own work very quickly.

And I should say, it wasn't perfect. It was a company growing extremely fast, and you could feel the growing pains. Processes were being invented in real time, and sometimes the pace of model releases outran the pace of understanding. But the thing I kept coming back to was that the people around me were uncomfortable with that gap too, and they were trying to close it rather than ignore it. That's what made me feel I was in the right place.

What interested me was how closely the research questions connected to building something people could actually use. With agents, especially, you need both: better underlying capabilities and a lot of care about how those capabilities behave in practice.
